question: A support operations lead must classify a large daily backlog of short inbound messages, and separately needs one deep analysis of a tangled contract dispute. Which two choices fit? Select two.
options: A) Use the deepest-reasoning tier for both of the jobs, since the strongest option is never bad.
B) Use the fastest, cheapest tier for both jobs, since the tiers differ mainly in reply speed.
C) Use the deepest-reasoning tier for the contract dispute, accepting the larger quota it uses.
D) Use the fastest, cheapest tier for the high-volume classification, where throughput matters.
E) Use whichever tier the team already has open, since the tier rarely changes what comes back.
correct_answers: C) Use the deepest-reasoning tier for the contract dispute, accepting the larger quota it uses.
D) Use the fastest, cheapest tier for the high-volume classification, where throughput matters.
explanations: Incorrect. Using the deepest tier for routine classification spends quota on work that does not need the extra reasoning depth.
Incorrect. The tiers differ in reasoning depth as well as speed, so the lightest tier is a poor fit for a tangled dispute.
Correct. A tangled one-off analysis is the case where deeper reasoning is worth the meaningfully larger quota it consumes.
Correct. High-volume, low-complexity classification is exactly where the fastest and cheapest tier earns its place.
Incorrect. Tier choice changes depth, speed and quota use, so treating it as incidental is how both of these jobs go wrong.
